analysis.one_liner: Bans petroleum refineries from using hydrofluoric acid, forcing a switch to safer alternatives.
analysis.headline: Referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on February 4, 2026; no hearing, vote, or further action has been taken.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Toxic Substances Control Act to make it illegal to use hydrogen fluoride (hydrofluoric acid) at petroleum refineries. New refineries could never use it, and existing ones would have five years to stop. It sets a $37,500 civil penalty per violation and blocks the EPA from waiving the rule. The bill's findings say about 40 U.S. refineries use the chemical and that a large release could kill or permanently injure thousands of people living within 25 miles.
analysis.who_benefits: The more than 14 million people the bill identifies as living in communities around the roughly 40 refineries that still use hydrofluoric acid, many of them communities that already carry heavy environmental burdens. Refinery workers also gain protection, since a release would injure them first.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People living near refineries using the acid

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits hydrofluoric acid at new refineries immediately and at existing refineries five years after enactment, removing the risk of a mass-casualty release in surrounding communities [S2].

The bill's findings state that more than 14 million people are at risk of death or permanent injury from living near these refineries, and that proven safer alternatives are already used by the majority of U.S. refineries [S2].
The bill sets a $37,500 civil penalty for each violation and forbids the EPA from issuing a waiver excusing a refinery from the ban [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The roughly 40 refinery owners still using the acid would pay to convert to alternative refining technology. Some of that cost could be passed to consumers through gasoline prices, though the bill's findings say the alternatives are commercially proven and already used by most refineries.
analysis.who_pays_short: Refinery owners still using the acid

drawbacks.text: Conversion is not free: the roughly 40 affected refineries would bear capital costs within five years, and some portion could show up in gasoline prices, though most U.S. refineries already run on the safer process [S2].

The $37,500 per-violation penalty is modest relative to a catastrophic release, so the bill's enforcement teeth are limited to that amount, which an honest supporter would acknowledge is small against potential harm [S2].
The bill provides no federal funding or compliance schedule flexibility beyond the five-year window, leaving operators to finance conversions on their own [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is large and one-sided in ordinary people's favor: the bill's own findings describe a potential mass-casualty event affecting thousands within 25 miles, against conversion costs for a minority of refineries to adopt technology most of the industry already uses. The main honest objections are the cost burden on the laggard refineries and a penalty level that may underdeter.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Energy and Commerce Committee, which has taken no action on it since, so it is sitting in committee with no vote scheduled.

narrative.text: Rep. Maxine Waters introduced the bill on February 4, 2026, joined by six Democratic cosponsors: Reps. Lieu, Barragan, Garcia of California, Tlaib, Norton, and Cohen [S2].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, which is the only action in its history; no hearing, markup, or floor vote has occurred [S4].

The bill's findings state that hydrofluoric acid is used in large quantities at about 40 U.S. refineries and that a major release could kill or permanently injure thousands of people within a 25-mile radius [S2].
The bill's findings state that safer, commercially proven alternatives are already used by the majority of U.S. refineries [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For now, the refinery operators that still use hydrofluoric acid, because no conversion requirement exists yet.

for.name: Maxine Waters
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban hydrofluoric acid at refineries.

for.name: 7 of 217 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction (Lieu, Barragan, Garcia of California, Tlaib, Norton, Cohen, plus the sponsor).

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on February 4, 2026 and has taken no further action on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: All seven sponsors and cosponsors are House Democrats and no Republican has joined; there has been no vote, so the partisan split is limited to sponsorship, not the record.

industries.note: The bill would force the roughly 40 refineries still using hydrofluoric acid to convert to safer technology within five years or stop using it, with a $37,500 penalty per violation and no waivers. Their interest in continuing the cheaper, more dangerous process runs against the safety of the 14 million people the bill says live in harm's way.

Suppliers of the commercially proven alternative alkylation technologies would gain customers as refiners convert, and their interest runs alongside community safety since the alternatives remove the release hazard.

analysis.trajectory: With no committee action since its February 2026 referral and no Republican support, the bill is following the usual path of a single-sponsor bill sent to a committee that never schedules it. Unless Energy and Commerce holds a hearing or markup before the Congress ends in January 2027, it will die without a vote.
